title: Plan a movement week around your actual calendar
summary: A paper-first planning exercise for busy adults, with a clear distinction between general guidelines and your next practical decision.
author: Form editorial source author (AI-assisted)

sections.heading: A guideline is context, not a calendar
paragraphs: CDC describes a general adult target of 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly and muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days. That is population guidance, not a requirement to begin at that amount or a personalized prescription.

Our worksheet begins somewhere different: an honest look at the week in front of you. Write down commitments that cannot move before adding anything. A blank calendar often describes a fantasy rather than a useful plan.

sections.heading: Pick a purpose you can describe
paragraphs: Choose one ordinary-life reason for making room for movement. It might be enjoying a walk with a friend, feeling more familiar with a gym, or reserving time away from a desk. This is your reason, not a predicted result.

Next to that purpose, write the available place, a realistic time window and any support you need. Keep travel and changing time in the same box. A twenty-minute opening may be consumed by a fifteen-minute journey.

sections.heading: Make two versions of the week
paragraphs: On paper, make an ordinary-week column and a disrupted-week column. The second column should account for a real obstacle: weather, travel, a caregiving change or an unavailable space. It is a planning alternative, not a punishment for missing the first version.
checklist: Ordinary week: available place, travel time, opening and support.
Disrupted week: which practical constraint changes?
End of week: what was feasible, and what should be revised?

sections.heading: Review the plan without grading your body
paragraphs: At the end of the week, compare your calendar with what happened. Record a constraint that was missing from the original plan and one decision that made participation easier. Avoid using a single difficult week as a verdict about your character.
This article does not assess fitness or provide individual health advice. If you have a condition or uncertainty about appropriate activity, discuss your plan with a qualified professional.
